papers.title_in_file: Shot-Based Quantum Encoding: A Data-Loading Paradigm for Quantum Neural Networks
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections I to VI (introduction, background, SBQE method, experiments, discussion, conclusion).
papers.what_it_is: A Terra Quantum paper that proposes shot-based quantum encoding (SBQE), which encodes data in the classical split of shots over initial states, and benchmarks it in simulation on three image datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report mean test accuracy of 80.95% on Fashion-MNIST and 90.25% on MNIST for SBQE, which is 2.0% and 2.1 percentage points above amplitude encoding respectively.
assertions.anchor: Section IV.C Results, p.5
quotes: SBQE again leads with 80.95%
outperforming amplitude encoding by an absolute 2.0% and the linear MLP by 1.3%
SBQE reaches 90.25%
by 2.1 percentage points and the width-matched classical network
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study by the method's authors, on a simulator, with 8 PCA features.
assertions.reader_inference: The width-matched classical network is within 0.3 points of SBQE on MNIST, so the result does not show a quantum advantage. The accuracies come from 8 PCA components, far below standard classical MNIST accuracy, and the runs are statevector simulations, not hardware.

assertions.value: The authors show that each SBQE layer is a linear map in the encoded probabilities, so that SBQE is structurally equivalent to a multilayer perceptron whose weights are realized by quantum circuits.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Section III.C Connection to multilayer perceptrons, p.3
quotes: We show that SBQE is structurally equivalent to a multilayer perceptron whose weights are realized by quantum circuits
Hence each layer is a linear map in the encoded probabilities
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived from the density-matrix formulation, Eqs. 8 to 10, Section III.C, p.3.
assertions.reader_inference: The equivalence says each layer is linear in the probabilities, so the nonlinearity and the learned probability map p(x) are classical.

assertions.value: The authors state that every configuration is run 10 times with independent parameter initialization, that each image is reduced to d = 8 principal components, and that the quantum models use nq = 8 qubits and nlayers = 4.
assertions.anchor: Section IV.A and IV.B, pp.4-5
quotes: Every configuration is run 10 times with independent parameter initialization, and metrics are averaged.
projected onto the first d = 8 principal components via PCA
We compare three architectures that share the same quantum workload (nq = 8 qubits, nlayers = 4)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup, Sections IV.A and IV.B.

assertions.value: The authors list limitations of SBQE: shot budgets grow with feature dimension if low-variance multinomial sampling is required, a probability mapping p(x) must be chosen for each dataset, and multilayer SBQE needs multiple sequential passes through the quantum device.
assertions.anchor: Section V Discussion, Limitations, pp.6-7
quotes: Shot budgets grow with feature dimension if one insists on low-variance multinomial sampling
The preprocessing step requires choosing an appropriate probability mapping p(x) for each dataset
Multilayer SBQE requires multiple sequential passes through the quantum device, which can be costly in wall-clock time
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own limitations, Section V, pp.6-7.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum-Evolutionary Neural Networks for Multi-Agent Federated Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract and Sections 1 to 7; reference list skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A short arXiv paper from two high-school authors that combines sine-activation (quantum-inspired) neural networks, local evolutionary mutation and federated averaging with added noise, tested on a synthetic dataset and on MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100.

assertions.value: The authors report that on a synthetic dataset with a 10-dimensional feature vector the best of ten mutated models reached accuracy 0.973 and the global model stabilizes around 0.97.
assertions.anchor: Section 5 Experimental Results, Table 1 and text, pp.9-10
quotes: Each data sample was composed of a 10-dimensional feature vector
mutation M1 achieved the highest accuracy at 0.973
the accuracy of the global model consistently improves and stabilizes around 0.97, while the loss decreases and plateaus near 0.1
assertions.certainty_reason: One synthetic-data experiment by the authors, with no external benchmark.
assertions.reader_inference: The label rule is a threshold on the sum of the features, a simple task. The paper gives no accuracy for the MNIST, CIFAR10 or CIFAR100 comparison in text, only in Fig. 4.

assertions.value: The authors state that the core layers are designed to simulate quantum interference, and that entanglement is emulated through stacked QuantumLayer blocks.
assertions.anchor: Section 3.2 and Section 4.2, pp.4-6
quotes: whose core layers are designed to simulate quantum interference via
We emulate this phenomenon through stacked QuantumLayer blocks in the QENN architecture
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of what its model is, Sections 3.2 and 4.2.
assertions.reader_inference: The model is a classical network with sine activations. No quantum circuit or hardware is used, so the abstract's phrase 'breakthrough in merging quantum computing' is not supported by an experiment here.

assertions.value: The authors state that the performance of the federated and baseline systems was quite close, with some degree of reduced accuracy in the federated case.
assertions.anchor: Section 6.2 Effectiveness against Datasets, p.11 (numbers are in Fig. 4 only)
quotes: the variations in performance between the federated and the baseline systems were quite close, which indicates that there is some degree of reduced accuracy
assertions.certainty_reason: Qualitative statement of an empirical result; the figures are only in an image.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no figure for the gap and no baseline for the quantum-inspired layers against ordinary activations.

assertions.value: The authors state that the model struggled with highly non-IID data distributions and was very sensitive to client dropout.
assertions.anchor: Section 6.1 Model Limitations, p.10
quotes: The model struggled with highly non-IID data distributions, where each agent only had access to a small biased subset of the overall dataset
the model was very sensitive to client dropout
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own limitations, Section 6.1, p.10.

papers.title_in_file: The cost of quantum algorithms for biochemistry: A case study in metaphosphate hydrolysis
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Preliminaries, Results (Section II, Table I), and Discussion (limitations, improvements, impact). The Methods sections (III.A to III.H) and the appendix were not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: A resource-estimation study of three ground-state-energy algorithms (ADAPT-VQE, quantum Krylov, quantum phase estimation) for metaphosphate hydrolysis, using exact simulation, numerical estimation and analytical bounds.

assertions.value: The authors report that variational methods, while being the most heuristic, still require substantially fewer overall resources on quantum hardware and could feasibly address such problems on current or near-future devices, and that the Trotter-based two-qubit gate counts of quantum Krylov and quantum phase estimation are well beyond current quantum computers.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Section II Results, pp.1 and 5
quotes: Our results show that variational methods, while being the most heuristic, still require substantially fewer overall resources on quantum hardware, and could feasibly address such problems on current or near-future devices.
the number of two-qubit gates is well-beyond the capabilities of current quantum computers
assertions.certainty_reason: Resource estimates from one study; ADAPT counts come from explicit simulation and the Krylov and QPE counts are bounds and estimates.
assertions.reader_inference: The ordering rests on counts that omit diagonalization circuits, state preparation, classical optimization cost and error correction (see the limitation assertion).

assertions.value: The authors report that a single Trotter step for the system H1 requires 6050622 single-qubit gates and 13016100 two-qubit gates, and for the system H2 requires 5351074 single-qubit gates and 11372404 two-qubit gates, assuming all-to-all connectivity.
assertions.anchor: Section II Results, p.4
quotes: For H1, a single Trotter step requires 6050622 single-qubit gates and 13016100 two-qubit gates.
For H2, a single Trotter step requires 5351074 single-qubit gates and 11372404 two-qubit gates.
As mentioned above, this assumes all-to-all connectivity
assertions.certainty_reason: Output of the authors' own compilation (Paulihedral) for one pair of Hamiltonians.
assertions.reader_inference: These are compiler outputs for first-order Trotter steps, so they depend on the compiler and the downfolded Hamiltonians.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in a minimal 6-31G(d) basis without explicit solvent molecules, the metaphosphate hydrolysis reaction involves 50 electrons in 78 orbitals.
assertions.anchor: Section I.A.1 Problem definitions, p.3
quotes: In a minimal, 6-31G(d) basis, not considering other solvent molecules explicitly, the reaction involves 50 electrons in 78 orbitals
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own problem setup, Section I.A.1, p.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that their gate counts do not include diagonalization circuits for energy estimation or initial state preparation, that resource counts include only quantum and not classical resources, and that circuits at this scale will require error correction and so additional overhead.
assertions.anchor: Section II (last paragraph) and Section IV.A Limitations, pp.5 and 11
quotes: Our gate counts in Table I do not include diagonalization circuits for energy estimation (in ADAPT-VQE and quantum Krylov), nor do they include initial state preparation
Our resource counts include only quantum and not classical resources.
We state these resources without regards to error correction, though it is certain that circuits at this scale will require error correction and so additional overhead.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own limitations, Section IV.A, p.11, and Section II, p.5.

papers.title_in_file: Hamiltonian Encoding for Quantum Approximate Time Evolution of Kinetic Energy Operator
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section IV (results and gate counts), Section V (complexity and error analysis) and Section VI (conclusion). The appendix proofs and the method sections were skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A paper that proposes quantum approximate time evolution (QATE) encoding and a quantum pyramid architecture to implement the kinetic energy operator as a diagonal unitary, tested on Qiskit simulators.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QATE circuit reaches a fidelity of 0.73 with 3 qubits and 0.99 with 9 or more qubits on the IBM Qasm simulator, against about 0.89 for the state-of-the-art method at 9 qubits.
assertions.anchor: Section IV (fidelity experiment before Section V), p.8
quotes: various measurement shots (depending on the qubit size) are performed on the IBM Qasm simulator
It is observed that our proposed quantum circuit possesses a fidelity of 0.73 with 3 qubits, and it reaches a fidelity of 0.99 with 9 or more qubits.
As compared to the state of the art (0.89 approximately with 9 qubits)
assertions.certainty_reason: One simulation study by the method's authors.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract says results were obtained on an IBM quantum machine, but the results section and the conclusion describe the IBM Qasm simulator and the IBM quantum simulator. A noiseless-simulator fidelity of 0.99 is not a hardware result.

assertions.value: The paper states in Lemma 3 that, for an n-qubit circuit, the QATE algorithm requires O(n) 1-qubit gates and n−1C2 + 2(n − 2) 2-qubit gates to design a bi-symmetric diagonal evolution operator.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, Lemma 3 and its proof, p.8
quotes: Lemma 3. Given an n-qubit quantum circuit, the QATE algorithm requires O(n) 1-qubit gate, and n−1C2 + 2(n − 2) number of 2-qubit gates to design a bi-symmetric diagonal evolution operator.
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 3 and its counting proof, Section IV, p.8.
assertions.reader_inference: The count n-1C2 of controlled-phase gates grows quadratically in n, which does not match the abstract's claim of subquadratic gate complexity. The paper itself says its 2-qubit gate count is similar to the existing method.

assertions.value: The authors report circuit depths for QATE of 9, 18, 22 and 36 at 3, 4, 5 and 6 qubits, against 16, 24, 32 and 40 for the existing approach.
assertions.anchor: Section IV.B Circuit depth, Table II, p.9
quotes: Qubit Size (n) 3 4 5 6 Existing approach [4] 16 24 32 40 Proposed QATE algorithm 9 18 22 36
assertions.certainty_reason: One compilation study by the authors in Qiskit.
assertions.reader_inference: The depths are transpiled circuit depths for 3 to 6 qubits only, so they do not show how the advantage scales.

assertions.value: The authors state that the number of 2-qubit gates is similar to the existing method, and that the application of the proposed QWE encoding is unknown at the moment.
assertions.anchor: Section IV.A Gate counts, p.9; Section VI Conclusion, p.10
quotes: The number of 2-qubit gates is similar to the existing method.
the application of the proposed QWE is unknown at the moment
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own limits, Section IV.A and Section VI.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks for Sequential Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 4 (experiments), Section 5 (conclusion). The architecture sections 2 and 3 were skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: A paper that proposes a fully quantum recurrent neural network built from hardware-efficient quantum recurrent blocks (pQRNN and staggered sQRNN) and tests it on meteorological data, stock prices and a small text-categorization task.

assertions.value: The authors report that both QRNN models are capable of predicting the five meteorological indicators and the five components of stock price with higher accuracy than the classical RNN.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.1 and 4.2, Tables 1 and 3, pp.17-19 (table values not quoted)
quotes: both two QRNN models are capable of predicting the five indicators with higher accuracy than the classical RNN
both two QRNN models are capable of predicting the five components of stock price with higher accuracy than the classical RNN
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study by the method's authors; numerical experiments only.
assertions.reader_inference: Accuracy is defined as one minus the mean squared relative error. The data are short series (the authors give 500 and 180 elements) and the paper reports no repeated runs or significance test.

assertions.value: The authors report that both QRNN models reach 100% accuracy on the MC text task (130 sentences; 100 for training and 30 for test), against 79.8% for the DisCoCat quantum model.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.3 Text categorization, Table 4, pp.20-21
quotes: The 130 sentences are divided into 100 for training and 30 for test.
both two QRNN models can achieve an accuracy of 100%, which is much better than that of the syntactic analysis-based quantum model [45]
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on a 30-sentence test set from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: With 30 test sentences and 17 words in the vocabulary the task is tiny, and the hybrid model QSANN also reaches 100%, so the comparison does not separate the models.

assertions.value: The authors state that each meteorological indicator has 500 elements split into 300 for training and 200 for test, that each stock component has 180 elements split into 100 for training and 80 for test, and that each task predicts the eighth day from the preceding seven days.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.1 and 4.2, pp.16 and 19
quotes: The 500 elements of each indicator are divided into 300 for training and 200 for test.
The 180 elements of each component are divided into 100 for training and 80 for test.
The task is to train the QRNN model to be capable of predicting the value of each indicator on the eighth day using the values of preceding seven days.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup, Sections 4.1 and 4.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that characterizing the trainability of the QRNNs, that is, the properties of barren plateau and landscape of cost functions, is future work, and that further work is required to clarify the limitation brought by the quantum gradient estimation.
assertions.anchor: Section 3 (gradient discussion), p.15; Section 5 Conclusion, p.21
quotes: characterizing the trainability of the QRNNs, i.e., the properties of barren plateau and landscape of cost functions
Further works are required to clarify the limitation brought by the quantum gradient estimation
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own open items, Section 5, p.21.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract says the QRNN is much more accessible on NISQ devices, but the experiments are numerical (pyQPanda) and the paper reports no hardware run.

papers.title_in_file: First Tree-like Quantum Data Structure: Quantum B+ Tree
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 4 (QRAM assumption and main theorem statements), Section 5 statements, Section 6 (experiments) and Section 8 (conclusion). The appendix proofs were not read.
papers.what_it_is: A database-theory paper that defines the quantum range query problem, proposes a quantum B+ tree with a global-classical local-quantum search, and compares memory-access counts with classical trees in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that their quantum B+ tree answers a static quantum range query in time that does not depend on the output size, asymptotically optimal in quantum computers and exponentially faster than classical B+ trees.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Theorem 4.4 (Section 4); Section 8 Conclusion
quotes: Since the execution time does not depend on the output size
which is asymptotically optimal in quantum computers and is exponentially faster than classical B+ trees
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 4.4 (average-case time) with Lemma 4.2 for optimality, Section 4; proofs in the appendix were not read.
assertions.reader_inference: The result holds only under the assumed ideal QRAM and counts QRAM accesses as unit cost, so it is a model result, not a wall-clock speedup.

assertions.value: The authors state that they assume the existence of a classical-write quantum-read QRAM, which is still discussed at the theoretical stage with no existing physical implementation yet available.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.1 Quantum Random Access Memory, p.4
quotes: we assume the existence of a classicalwrite quantum-read QRAM
no existing physical implementation is yet available
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of the assumption its results rest on, Section 4.1.
assertions.reader_inference: Every complexity result in the paper depends on this assumption.

assertions.value: The authors report that, counting memory accesses on the Brightkite and Gowalla datasets, the quantum B+ tree is up to 1000x more efficient than the classical B+ tree for static quantum range queries, and that they chose not to verify quantum supremacy.
assertions.anchor: Section 6 Experiment, Effect of the dataset size, p.9
quotes: we chose to evaluate the number of memory accesses to make the comparisons
it is up to 1000x more efficient than the classical B+ tree for the (static) quantum range queries
Thus, in this paper, we would not verify the quantum supremacy
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated memory-access counts from one study by the authors, not run times.
assertions.reader_inference: The 1000x figure compares counted QRAM accesses under the model, so it restates the asymptotic claim and says nothing about hardware speed.

assertions.value: The authors report that the dynamic quantum B+ tree needs 3x more memory accesses for insertion or deletion than the classical B+ tree.
assertions.anchor: Section 6 Experiment, Effect of the dataset size, p.9
quotes: the dynamic quantum B+ tree needs 3x more memory accesses for insertion or deletion
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated memory-access counts from one study by the authors.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper also says the dynamic quantum tree has more accesses than the classical tree for small datasets, so the advantage appears only at larger sizes.

papers.title_in_file: Continuous-variable photonic quantum extreme learning machines for fast collider-data selection
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 4 (results), Section 5 (summary and conclusions). Section 3 (CV-QELM construction) was skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A paper that studies continuous-variable photonic quantum extreme learning machines as fast front-ends for collider data, comparing a fixed Gaussian random feature map with a linear readout against parameter-matched MLPs on top-jet tagging and Higgs identification.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the hls4ml LHC jet dataset with F = 16 engineered features the CV-QELM consistently outperformed the H = 2 MLP across all training sizes, with the largest margin in the low-statistics regime.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.1 and Section 5, pp.12-16
quotes: For the hls4ml LHC jet dataset with F = 16 engineered features, the CV-QELM consistently outperformed the H = 2 MLP across all training sizes, with the largest margin in the low-statistics regime.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on public data, with a two-hidden-unit baseline.
assertions.reader_inference: The H = 2 baseline is a very small network chosen by parameter matching, so the result shows an advantage over a tiny MLP, not over a well-tuned classical model.

assertions.value: The authors report that the CV-QELM also surpasses the wider H = 10 MLP on jet tagging, and that on the Higgs task ridge regression yielded results marginally below the H = 10 model but above the H = 2 baseline.
assertions.anchor: Section 5 Summary and Conclusions, pp.15-16; Figs. 4 to 8
quotes: the CV-QELM also surpasses the wider H = 10 MLP
ridge regression yielded results marginally below the H = 10 model but above the H = 2 baseline
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; the figures are only in images.
assertions.reader_inference: Against the wider MLP the outcome depends on the readout and on the dataset, so the abstract's phrase 'matches or exceeds' is a mixed picture.

assertions.value: The authors state that for these studies F = M with a single feature embedded on each qumode, and that the MLP baselines are trained with cross-entropy loss, early stopping, and a small grid search over weight decay.
assertions.anchor: Section 4 Results, pp.10-12
quotes: for the studies conducted in this paper, we will use F = M and embed a single feature on each qumode
The MLP baselines are trained with cross-entropy loss, early stopping, and a small grid search over weight decay.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup, Section 4.

assertions.value: The authors name hardware co-design and on-bench validation of latency, power, and noise characteristics as a natural next step.
assertions.anchor: Section 5 Summary and Conclusions, p.16
quotes: A natural next step is hardware co-design and on-bench validation of latency, power, and noise characteristics
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this as an open next step, Section 5, p.16.
assertions.reader_inference: The nanosecond-scale latency, low power and room-temperature claims in the abstract and conclusion are therefore design arguments, not measured results.

papers.title_in_file: QDC: Quantum Diffusion Convolution Kernels on Graphs
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 5 (experiments), Section 6 (conclusion). The method sections were skimmed and the appendix was not read.
papers.what_it_is: A CashApp paper that proposes a graph convolution kernel based on the propagation of a quantum particle over a graph (QDC), computed with classical eigensolvers, and tests it on nine node-classification datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report that QDC provides improvements in accuracy across the heterophilic datasets but seems to give mixed results for Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed, and that MultiScaleQDC appears to provide improvements across all datasets.
assertions.anchor: Section 5 Experiments, Node Classification, Table 1, p.8
quotes: We observe that QDC provides improvements in accuracy across the heterophilic datasets, but seems to provide mixed results for Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed.
By using MultiScaleQDC, we see that multi-scale modeling appears to provide improvements across all datasets.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study by the method's author, against baselines the author tuned.
assertions.reader_inference: The gains are largest on heterophilic graphs and absent or negative on the homophilic ones for plain QDC. The method runs on classical hardware, so this is a quantum-inspired result.

assertions.value: The authors state that they evaluated on 9 data sets, ran 250 steps of hyper-parameter optimization for each method, and compared QDC with GDC and SDRL and an unprocessed Laplacian in both a GCN and a GAT.
assertions.anchor: Section 5 Experiments, Experiment Setup and Datasets, p.8
quotes: We performed 250 steps of hyper-parameter optimization for each method
We evaluated our method on 9 data sets
so we have chosen to compare QDC to both GDC and SDRL in addition to an unprocessed Laplacian in both a GCN and a GAT
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup, Section 5, p.8.

assertions.value: The authors state that all computations were run on an Nvidia DGX A100 machine with 128 AMD Rome 7742 cores and 8 Nvidia A100 GPUs.
assertions.anchor: Section 5 Experiments, Experiment Setup, p.8
quotes: all computations were run on an Nvidia DGX A100 machine with 128 AMD Rome 7742 cores and 8 Nvidia A100 GPUs
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own compute setup, Section 5, p.8.
assertions.reader_inference: All results come from classical GPU computation, so the quantum dynamics are simulated by classical eigensolvers and no quantum device is involved.

assertions.value: The authors state that the method is still more expensive than spatial convolutions, that propagating gradients through approximate eigensolvers is quite challenging, and that because the method is spectral it can be used only in transductive settings.
assertions.anchor: Section 6 Conclusion, pp.10-11
quotes: our method is still more expensive than spatial convolutions
propagating gradients through approximate eigensolvers is quite challenging
because our method is spectral, we are only able to use this method in transductive settings
assertions.certainty_reason: The author states the method's limits, Section 6, pp.10-11.
